patient.name: Sanjay Patel
patient.complaint: Burning chest pain after meals and at night for 3 months
background: Minicab driver in Wembley; eats his main meal at 11 pm after shifts
Drinks 4 cups of coffee a day
No other medical history; no regular medicines

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with heartburn after meals, worse lying down, sometimes with atypical cough or hoarseness, or a complication question (Barrett's, stricture, adenocarcinoma).

points: Sanjay, 48, has **burning behind his breastbone** after meals.
Worse when he **lies down** after his late dinner.
Sour fluid comes up into his mouth at night.
He wakes coughing; his voice is hoarse in the mornings.

visual.title: Sanjay's 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Normal sinus rhythm, no ST changes. Always exclude a cardiac cause of chest pain first.

steps.text: Burning chest pain needs an ECG before you call it reflux.

steps.lead: Sanjay has the classic trio: **heartburn after eating**, **regurgitation** and pain lying down, plus cough and hoarseness from acid reaching his larynx.
Acid is escaping past Sanjay's **lower oesophageal sphincter** into his oesophagus.
He is **obese** and **smokes**; in a woman, **pregnancy** would be a classic risk too.

steps.q: Which feature would make Sanjay's chest pain most likely to be cardiac rather than reflux?
o: Pain on exertion relieved by rest
steps.r: **Exertional** pain relieved by rest is angina. Meal-related, positional burning with a sour taste is reflux.

steps.title: Burning chest or upper abdominal pain
head: Feature
GORD
Angina / ACS
Peptic ulcer

steps.lead: Years of acid could give Sanjay **Barrett's oesophagus**, a **stricture** or **oesophageal adenocarcinoma**.

steps.text: New **dysphagia** in a patient with long-standing reflux is a red flag: think stricture or adenocarcinoma, not just worse GORD.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (a clinical diagnosis with H. pylori testing if no red flags) or when to refer for endoscopy (red flags, age 55 or over, failed treatment).

steps.q: Sanjay is 48 with no red flags. Does he need an endoscopy now?
o: No: clinical diagnosis, test for H. pylori and treat
steps.r: Under 55 with no red flags, **GORD is a clinical diagnosis**. Offer H. pylori testing and start treatment.

steps.lead: Sanjay's history is enough to diagnose GORD; **endoscopy** is kept for when confirmation is needed.
Sanjay has a **carbon-13 urea breath test** (negative), then starts **omeprazole** and keeps a meal diary.

steps.title: Dyspepsia and reflux work-up
nodes: None → urea breath test for H. pylori
No response >4 weeks or age ≥55 → endoscopy

points: 8 weeks later: still heartburn most nights despite omeprazole.
No weight loss, no dysphagia, no bleeding.

steps.lead: Sanjay's symptoms persist **despite treatment**, so he gets an OGD; he **stops omeprazole 2 weeks before** so acid damage is not masked.

visual.title: Sanjay's age against the endoscopy threshold
bands: Under 55: test and treat if no red flags
visual.label: Sanjay 48
visual.caption: Below 55, so his OGD was triggered by failed treatment, not age.

steps.title: Sanjay's OGD and biopsy
rows: Linear erosions, LA grade B oesophagitis

steps.text: A **barium swallow** does not replace endoscopy for GORD: it cannot biopsy or show Barrett's.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (lifestyle plus a PPI) or 'next step' after partial response (higher dose or switch PPI, add an H2 antagonist, then fundoplication).

steps.lead: Sanjay needs to **lose weight**, stop eating at 11 pm, **raise the head of his bed** and take **omeprazole**.

steps.q: Which piece of lifestyle advice best targets Sanjay's night-time symptoms?
o: Drink a glass of milk at bedtime
Eat his main meal 3 hours before bed
Take ibuprofen for the chest pain
steps.r: **Avoiding late meals** and raising the bed head stop acid pooling at the LOS overnight. NSAIDs worsen dyspepsia.

visual.title: Sanjay's heartburn nights per week
visual.caption: Partial response on omeprazole; better after switching to lansoprazole and adding famotidine at night.

steps.lead: Sanjay's partial response leads to **lansoprazole**; nocturnal symptoms then settle when **famotidine** is added at night.

steps.title: GORD treatment ladder
nodes: Lifestyle: weight, late meals, bed head, smoking
Inadequate: increase dose or switch to lansoprazole

steps.lead: Sanjay's care follows **NICE dyspepsia and GORD** guidance; any red flag would mean a **2-week wait** referral.
If Sanjay's reflux stayed severe despite all of this, a **fundoplication** would be the rare surgical option.

steps.text: Stopping **smoking**, cutting caffeine and alcohol and losing weight all improve LOS function: lifestyle is always part of the answer.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: how a PPI works, why pregnancy or hiatus hernia worsens reflux, and which change occurs in Barrett's oesophagus (columnar metaplasia).

steps.lead: Sanjay's **LOS** does not close properly, so acid flows backwards into his oesophagus.
Sanjay's small **sliding hiatus hernia** pulls the GOJ above the diaphragm and weakens his barrier; in pregnancy **progesterone** relaxes the LOS.

steps.title: From reflux to cancer
steps.caption: Squamous epithelium is replaced by acid-resistant columnar epithelium.

steps.lead: If Sanjay's oesophagitis continues for years, his squamous lining may switch to **columnar** cells: **Barrett's**.

steps.q: How does Sanjay's omeprazole reduce acid?
steps.r: PPIs **irreversibly block the proton pump** on parietal cells. Famotidine blocks H2 receptors; antacids neutralise.

steps.lead: With acid secretion cut, Sanjay's inflamed oesophagus can **heal**.

visual.title: Sanjay's BMI
visual.label: Sanjay 33
visual.caption: Obesity raises intra-abdominal pressure and pushes gastric contents up past the LOS.

steps.text: Barrett's is **metaplasia** (one mature cell type replaced by another), not dysplasia. Dysplasia is the next, precancerous step.

mcq.q: Which structure is defective in GORD?
mcq.r: A defective **lower oesophageal sphincter** lets acid reflux.

mcq.q: Which hormone explains reflux in pregnancy?
mcq.r: **Progesterone** relaxes smooth muscle, including the LOS.

mcq.q: Which is the classic symptom of GORD?
Which premalignant complication can long-standing GORD cause?
Which test for H. pylori is offered first-line in dyspepsia?
How long before endoscopy should omeprazole be stopped?
mcq.r: **2 weeks**, so it does not mask findings.

mcq.q: Which is a red flag that warrants urgent endoscopy?
mcq.r: **Dysphagia**, weight loss, GI bleeding and anaemia are red flags.

mcq.q: Which is the first-line drug for GORD?
Which surgery is used for refractory GORD?
mcq.r: **Fundoplication** wraps the fundus around the lower oesophagus.
They irreversibly inhibit the **H+/K+ ATPase** of parietal cells.

technique.stem: A 45 year old woman has a 2 month history of burning retrosternal pain that comes on after large meals and is worse when she lies down. She has an acid taste in her mouth at night. She is overweight. The pain does not occur on exertion. Her ECG and troponin are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Chest pain diagnosis: rule out the heart, then look at the triggers.
Burning, meal-related, positional, regurgitation, obese; cardiac tests normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **GORD**.

elim: Normal ECG and troponin and no exertional pain.
Biliary colic is RUQ pain after fatty meals, not positional heartburn.
Oesophageal spasm gives intermittent severe squeezing pain with dysphagia.
Pericarditis is sharp pain eased by sitting forward, with ECG changes.

steps.x: **D. GORD.** Burning + meals + lying down + sour taste.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man has had heartburn and regurgitation for 3 months. He has taken omeprazole 20 mg daily for 6 weeks with little benefit. He has no weight loss, dysphagia or bleeding. His GP books a routine upper GI endoscopy in 6 weeks and a repeat H. pylori test.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate advice before the endoscopy?
o: Continue omeprazole at the same dose

steps.x: It asks about **preparation** for endoscopy.

clues: omeprazole 20 mg daily for 6 weeks with little benefit
steps.x: Age and failed treatment justify OGD; a PPI would mask findings and H. pylori.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Stop omeprazole 2 weeks before**.

elim: Continuing the PPI can heal lesions and give false negative H. pylori tests.
A higher dose masks findings even more.
Only a few hours of fasting are needed.
No antibiotic before diagnosis.

steps.x: **E. Stop omeprazole 2 weeks before.** Off PPI so the scope sees the truth.

technique.stem: A 39 year old man has had severe GORD for 4 years. Despite weight loss, high-dose lansoprazole and night-time famotidine he still has daily regurgitation. Endoscopy shows oesophagitis without Barrett's, and 24-hour pH monitoring confirms acid reflux. He wants a long-term solution.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management of reflux that has failed medical treatment.
Every rung of the medical ladder tried; reflux is proven.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Laparoscopic fundoplication**.

elim: Metoclopramide is not part of the GORD ladder and has neurological side effects.
EMR treats dysplasia or early cancer; there is none.
Oesophagectomy is for cancer.
Stopping the PPI will make him worse.

steps.x: **C. Fundoplication.** Refractory, proven reflux = surgery.

technique.stem: A 52 year old man with 10 years of GORD has an upper GI endoscopy. There is salmon-pink mucosa extending 3 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction. Biopsy shows the normal stratified squamous epithelium replaced by columnar epithelium with goblet cells. There is no dysplasia.
technique.q: Which pathological process does this represent?

steps.x: A **pathological process** question: name the cell change.

clues: squamous epithelium replaced by columnar epithelium
steps.x: One mature epithelium replaced by another: Barrett's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Metaplasia**: squamous to columnar.

elim: Atrophy is shrinkage of cells or tissue.
The biopsy says no dysplasia.
Hyperplasia is more of the same cells.
There is no squamous neoplasia; the new cells are columnar.

steps.x: **B. Columnar metaplasia.** Barrett's: acid-resistant cells replace squamous.

practice.stem: A 44 year old man has a 6 week history of burning central chest pain after meals, worse when he bends or lies down, with a sour taste in his mouth. He is obese and smokes. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Normal sinus rhythm with no ST or T wave changes.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Burning chest pain after meals, worse bending or lying, with regurgitation in an obese smoker is GORD. A normal ECG and troponin make ACS unlikely.

steps.x: Chest pain diagnosis: heart first, then gut.

clues: burning central chest pain after meals
worse when he bends or lies down
steps.x: Classic heartburn and regurgitation with risk factors; ECG normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **GORD**.

elim: Achalasia causes dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start.
ECG and troponin are normal and the pain is meal-related.
Biliary colic is RUQ pain, not positional heartburn.
Peptic ulcer pain is epigastric and gnawing, not positional with regurgitation.

steps.x: **D. GORD.** Heartburn + positional + regurgitation.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant has burning retrosternal discomfort after meals and when lying flat at night. She has no headache, visual disturbance or right upper quadrant pain. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. Urinalysis shows no protein.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Heartburn after meals and lying flat in pregnancy is reflux: progesterone relaxes the LOS. Normal BP, no proteinuria and normal LFTs and platelets exclude pre-eclampsia and HELLP.

steps.x: Upper GI symptoms in pregnancy: exclude the dangerous causes first.

clues: no headache, visual disturbance or right upper quadrant pain
steps.x: Typical heartburn; no features of pre-eclampsia; labs are normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Reflux (GORD)** from progesterone and the gravid uterus.

elim: AFLP causes vomiting, jaundice and deranged LFTs.
Biliary colic is RUQ pain after fatty food.
HELLP needs haemolysis, raised ALT and low platelets.
BP is normal and there is no proteinuria.

steps.x: **E. Reflux oesophagitis.** Pregnancy is a classic GORD risk factor.

practice.stem: A 51 year old non-smoking man has a 4 month dry cough and hoarse voice, worst at night and after late meals. He also gets occasional heartburn. Chest X-ray and spirometry are normal. He takes no regular medicines. ENT examination shows a red, swollen posterior larynx.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Chronic cough and hoarseness worse at night and after meals, with heartburn and posterior laryngeal inflammation, is extra-oesophageal GORD.

steps.x: Chronic cough diagnosis: look for the gut clue.

clues: worst at night and after late meals
steps.x: Atypical GORD: acid irritates the larynx when lying down.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **GORD** with laryngopharyngeal symptoms.

elim: Normal spirometry and a meal link make asthma less likely.
ILD shows crackles and abnormal imaging.
Laryngeal cancer is linked to smoking and shows a mass, not diffuse posterior redness.
Sarcoid gives hilar nodes on X-ray.

steps.x: **B. GORD.** Cough + hoarseness + meals + lying down.

practice.stem: A 57 year old man has had GORD for 15 years. Upper GI endoscopy shows tongues of salmon-pink mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction. Biopsy shows columnar epithelium with goblet cells and no dysplasia.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Columnar metaplasia with goblet cells replacing squamous epithelium above the GOJ after long-standing reflux is Barrett's oesophagus, a precursor of adenocarcinoma.

steps.x: A complication of long-standing reflux on OGD.
Classic endoscopic and histological Barrett's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Barrett's oesophagus**.

elim: Eosinophilic oesophagitis shows rings and eosinophils, often with food bolus obstruction.
No dysplasia or mass, so not cancer.
Candidiasis gives white plaques, usually with immunosuppression.
The cells are columnar, not dysplastic squamous.

steps.x: **A. Barrett's oesophagus.** Salmon-pink + columnar + goblet cells.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man with 20 years of untreated GORD has 3 months of progressive difficulty swallowing solids, now also soft food, and 6 kg weight loss. He is obese and a former smoker. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Rapidly progressive dysphagia with weight loss after long-standing GORD is oesophageal adenocarcinoma via Barrett's. Squamous cell carcinoma links to smoking and alcohol in the upper and middle oesophagus.

steps.x: A complication of long-standing reflux with red flags.
Reflux, obesity, progressive dysphagia and weight loss; anaemia on labs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oesophageal adenocarcinoma**.

elim: Achalasia causes dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start.
A benign stricture is slow, without marked weight loss or anaemia.
SCC is linked to heavy smoking and alcohol, not GORD.
A pouch causes regurgitation of old food and halitosis.

steps.x: **C. Oesophageal adenocarcinoma.** GORD → Barrett's → adenocarcinoma.

practice.stem: A 71 year old woman with many years of poorly controlled reflux has 2 years of slowly worsening difficulty swallowing meat and bread. Her heartburn has recently become less troublesome. Her weight is stable. Endoscopy shows a smooth, short, concentric narrowing in the distal oesophagus, and biopsies are benign.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Long-standing reflux scars the distal oesophagus into a smooth benign peptic stricture, with slow dysphagia to solids and stable weight. Biopsies exclude cancer.

steps.x: A reflux complication with dysphagia: benign or malignant?
Slow, solids only, no weight loss, smooth and benign.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Benign peptic stricture**.

elim: Achalasia shows a dilated oesophagus with a tight LOS and liquid dysphagia.
Biopsies are benign and weight is stable.
A pouch is in the pharynx, with regurgitation and halitosis.
Plummer-Vinson is an upper web with iron deficiency.

steps.x: **B. Benign peptic stricture.** Slow + smooth + benign biopsy.

practice.stem: A 60 year old man has 2 months of new indigestion, upper abdominal discomfort and 5 kg unintentional weight loss. He has had reflux for years. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Red flags (weight loss, iron deficiency anaemia, age 55 or over) mean urgent 2-week wait endoscopy. A breath test is only for patients with no red flags.

steps.x: Initial investigation: check for **red flags** first.
Over 55, weight loss, anaemia on labs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent OGD**.

elim: Barium cannot biopsy.
CT stages cancer after diagnosis.
Manometry is for motility disorders.
Test-and-treat is only for patients with no red flags.

steps.x: **E. Urgent upper GI endoscopy.** Red flags skip test-and-treat.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman has 6 weeks of heartburn after meals and acid regurgitation. She has no weight loss, dysphagia, vomiting or bleeding. She has not taken any acid-suppressing medicine. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. Abdominal examination is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Under 55 with no red flags, GORD is a clinical diagnosis: offer a carbon-13 urea breath test for H. pylori and start treatment. Endoscopy is for red flags or failed treatment.

steps.x: Initial investigation in uncomplicated reflux.

clues: no weight loss, dysphagia, vomiting or bleeding
steps.x: Young, typical, no red flags; off PPI so the breath test is valid.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Carbon-13 urea breath test**.

elim: pH monitoring is for refractory or atypical cases, often before surgery.
Barium is for structural or motility questions, not first-line.
Chest X-ray does not help reflux.
Endoscopy is for red flags, age 55 or over, or failed treatment.

steps.x: **C. Urea breath test.** No red flags = test and treat.

practice.stem: A 40 year old man has 2 months of heartburn after late evening meals and regurgitation when lying down. He has a BMI of 32 and drinks 5 cups of coffee a day. He has no red flag symptoms and a urea breath test is negative.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: First-line GORD treatment is lifestyle modification (weight loss, avoiding late meals, raising the bed head, cutting caffeine) plus a PPI such as omeprazole.

steps.x: **Initial** management of uncomplicated GORD.
Modifiable triggers, no red flags, H. pylori negative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lifestyle advice plus a PPI**.

elim: An H2 antagonist is added later if symptoms persist on a PPI.
Surgery is for refractory cases.
Metoclopramide is not on the GORD ladder.
No red flags, so no urgent scope.

steps.x: **C. Lifestyle advice and omeprazole.**

practice.stem: A 46 year old woman has GORD. She has taken omeprazole for 8 weeks with only a partial response, despite good adherence and lifestyle changes. Upper GI endoscopy last month showed mild oesophagitis only, and she is H. pylori negative. She has no red flags.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: With an inadequate PPI response, increase the dose or try another PPI such as lansoprazole. Surgery is reserved for cases refractory to the whole medical ladder.

steps.x: Next step after partial response to first-line.
Endoscopy done and reassuring; climb one rung of the ladder.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Change PPI (lansoprazole)** or increase the dose.

elim: Metoclopramide is not part of the ladder.
Too early: medical options remain.
Stopping will worsen symptoms.
She had a scope last month and has no red flags.

steps.x: **D. Switch to lansoprazole.** Second-line: change or increase the PPI.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man with endoscopically confirmed mild reflux oesophagitis takes high-dose lansoprazole. Daytime symptoms are controlled but he still wakes with heartburn most nights. He sleeps with the bed head raised and eats early. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: Persistent symptoms, especially at night, despite a PPI are treated by adding an H2 receptor antagonist such as famotidine. Fundoplication is for refractory disease.

steps.x: Next step for persistent symptoms on a PPI.

clues: bed head raised and eats early
steps.x: Nocturnal breakthrough on optimised PPI and lifestyle.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Add an H2 antagonist (famotidine)**.

elim: Surgery comes after the medical ladder fails.
Already confirmed on endoscopy, no red flags.
Stopping the PPI loses daytime control.
Antacids alone are weaker than his current treatment.

steps.x: **A. Add famotidine at night.**

practice.stem: A 42 year old woman with GORD starts omeprazole. After 4 weeks her heartburn has resolved. Her endoscopic oesophagitis has healed on repeat endoscopy. She asks how the tablet works.
practice.q: Which is the mechanism of action of her medication?
o: Irreversible inhibition of the H+/K+ ATPase
practice.e: Omeprazole irreversibly inhibits the H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) on parietal cells, cutting acid secretion so the mucosa can heal. Famotidine blocks H2 receptors.

steps.x: Drug mechanism: which class is omeprazole?
A PPI, which allows healing by cutting acid.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Irreversible proton pump (H+/K+ ATPase) inhibition**.

elim: H2 blockade is famotidine.
D2 antagonism is metoclopramide or domperidone.
Neutralisation is antacids.
A PGE1 analogue is misoprostol.

steps.x: **C. H+/K+ ATPase inhibition.**

glossary.GORD: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: symptoms or damage from stomach contents flowing back into the oesophagus.
glossary.lower oesophageal sphincter: Muscle ring at the bottom of the oesophagus that stops stomach contents flowing back up.
glossary.heartburn: Burning pain behind the breastbone caused by acid in the oesophagus.
glossary.regurgitation: Stomach contents coming back up into the mouth without vomiting.
glossary.dysphagia: Difficulty swallowing; a red flag in reflux disease.
glossary.hoarseness: A rough or strained voice, here from acid irritating the larynx.
glossary.hiatus hernia: Part of the stomach pushed up through the diaphragm's oesophageal opening.
glossary.GOJ: Gastro-oesophageal junction, where the oesophagus joins the stomach.
glossary.progesterone: Pregnancy hormone that relaxes smooth muscle, including the LOS.
glossary.Barrett's oesophagus: Replacement of oesophageal squamous lining by columnar cells due to reflux; premalignant.
glossary.metaplasia: One mature cell type replaced by another better suited to a hostile environment.
glossary.columnar epithelium: Tall, column-shaped lining cells, like those of the stomach and intestine.
glossary.dysplasia: Disordered, abnormal cell growth that can progress to cancer.
glossary.adenocarcinoma: Cancer of glandular cells; the oesophageal cancer linked to reflux and Barrett's.
glossary.stricture: Narrowing of the oesophagus from scarring.
glossary.achalasia: Failure of the LOS to relax with loss of peristalsis, causing dysphagia to solids and liquids.
glossary.red flags: Warning features (weight loss, dysphagia, bleeding, anaemia) needing urgent endoscopy.
glossary.endoscopy: A camera passed into the gut to look and take biopsies.
glossary.OGD: Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy: endoscopy of the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum.
glossary.carbon-13 urea breath test: Breath test detecting H. pylori, which splits labelled urea into labelled CO2.
glossary.H. pylori: Helicobacter pylori, a stomach bacterium causing gastritis and ulcers.
glossary.PPI: Proton pump inhibitor, such as omeprazole or lansoprazole; blocks acid secretion.
glossary.omeprazole: A proton pump inhibitor; first-line drug for GORD.
glossary.lansoprazole: An alternative proton pump inhibitor tried when omeprazole works poorly.
glossary.H2 receptor antagonist: Drug such as famotidine that blocks histamine-driven acid secretion.
glossary.famotidine: H2 receptor antagonist added for persistent, often night-time, reflux.
glossary.H+/K+ ATPase: The proton pump on parietal cells that secretes stomach acid.
glossary.parietal cells: Stomach lining cells that secrete acid and intrinsic factor.
glossary.fundoplication: Surgery wrapping the gastric fundus around the lower oesophagus to stop reflux.
glossary.24-hour pH monitoring: A probe measuring oesophageal acid over a day to prove reflux.
glossary.antacids: Alkaline medicines that neutralise stomach acid for quick relief.
glossary.test and treat: Testing for H. pylori and treating it before endoscopy in patients without red flags.
glossary.2-week wait: NHS urgent suspected cancer referral, seen within two weeks.
